1 1번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Few foods reach as far back in time as noodles do. They are among the oldest dishes that can be found across cultures. No one can say for certain who first invented them. Nor is it clear when they were invented at all. What is certain is that they have been part of the human diet for thousands of years. Like any other food item, noodles are cooked and enjoyed in different ways in different cultures. Exploring the noodle dishes of the world therefore becomes a genuine learning experience. A short culinary tour from Italy to Peru is about to begin.
①the scientific method used to date the earliest wheat products
②the great age of noodles and the cultural variety in how they are eaten
③the reasons Italian noodles spread more widely than any other kind
④the health benefits of including noodles in a daily diet
⑤the difficulty of cooking traditional noodles at home
2 2번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Pasta, typically made of wheat flour, is a staple food in Italian cuisine. Nobody can say exactly when people began eating it. It is believed, however, that the food originated in Sicily and spread through the rest of Italy in the 17th century. It comes in a great many shapes and sizes, and each one carries its own name. Macaroni, lasagna and spaghetti are only three of them. Italians cook it with the recipes they love best, boiling the noodles first and building a sauce afterwards. Olive oil, garlic, chopped vegetables, sliced meat, herbs and tomatoes all find their way into the pot. Whatever the ingredients, they hold to the saying that at the table with good friends and family one does not age.
①the economic importance of wheat farming in southern Italy
②the correct way to boil noodles so that they keep their shape
③the rivalry between Sicilian cooking and northern Italian cooking
④pasta as an Italian staple, its origin and forms, and the value Italians place on the table
⑤the reasons tomatoes became the most common pasta ingredient

3 3번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Pho is a Vietnamese rice noodle dish eaten for breakfast all over the country. Vietnam ranks among the largest rice-producing countries in the world. Its growing conditions for rice are close to ideal. No wonder steamed rice is a main staple food in Vietnamese cuisine. The same rice is also made into noodles, which are served in a bowl of chicken, beef or seafood broth. Spices and herbs give that broth a distinct Vietnamese flavor. Variations depend on the ingredients or on the type of broth used. The two best known are one served in beef broth and one served in chicken broth.
①how Vietnam's rice-growing conditions shaped a national noodle dish and its varieties
②the difficulty of exporting Vietnamese rice to other countries
③the reasons breakfast is the largest meal of the day in Vietnam
④the medicinal properties of the herbs used in Vietnamese cooking
⑤the competition between beef broth and chicken broth among Vietnamese cooks
4 4번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Among the dishes that Algerians name first, rechta stands near the top. Its name goes back to the Persian word rishta, a term meaning "thread," which is generally applied to noodles produced from wheat flour. The noodles themselves are rolled thin and pressed flat rather than round. Cooks in Algeria prepare them by working wheat flour, salt, water, and ghee, a clarified butter, into a single dough. Around the noodles go chopped meat, onions, garlic, turnips, potatoes, zucchini, and spices found nowhere else. Families bring the dish out for celebrations, weddings above all, and for Eid al-Fitr, which closes the month of Ramadan. One detail is easy to overlook: no pork ever enters the pot. Islamic dietary law counts pork as haram, or forbidden, rather than halal, or permissible, and the recipe follows that rule.
①the health benefits of cooking with clarified butter
②the spread of Persian vocabulary through North African languages
③the reasons wheat replaced rice as Algeria's leading crop
④how Algerian weddings differ from weddings elsewhere in Africa
⑤what rechta is made of and the cultural rules that shape it

5 5번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Lunch and dinner tables across Peru often carry a bowl of sopa criolla. Peruvians treat it as comfort food, and many households keep it in steady rotation. The name translates as "creole soup," and creole points to local people who usually descend from European conquerors. That single word hints at something larger about the country's cooking. Peruvian cuisine has been shaped not just by indigenous ethnic groups but also by settlers who arrived from abroad. The soup itself begins with thin noodles that cooks often call "angel hair." Those noodles are boiled and ladled into a bowl of beef stock seasoned with garlic, onions, tomato paste, and milk. A fried egg is set on top, which makes the dish look and taste delicious to Peruvians of every age.
①the difficulty of finding thin noodles in South American markets
②the nutritional advantages of adding eggs to soup
③how a familiar Peruvian soup reflects the mixed origins of the country's cuisine
④the history of European conquest in South America
⑤why Peruvians prefer soup to other kinds of lunch
6 6번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Noodle dishes turn out to be as varied as the cultures that enjoy them. No two places prepare a bowl in quite the same way. That variety is worth meeting in person rather than reading about. So on your next visit to another country, order a noodle dish there. Let the bowl lead you toward the culture standing behind it. As you eat, something familiar will surface underneath the unfamiliar flavors. You will see that all humans have something in common. Even so, a question may stay with you: why are noodles popular around the world?
①how tasting another country's noodles reveals both cultural variety and shared humanity
②the importance of asking questions while studying history
③the reason certain countries produce more wheat than others
④why travelers should learn to cook before going abroad
⑤the growing popularity of international restaurants at home

7 7번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
A rivalry between two restaurants only a hundred feet apart once turned into a hospital-room encounter neither side expected. The owner responsible for the accident arrived with nothing more than an apology and a basket of pastries. The patient could not yet forgive her, but he still described every flavor she had hidden inside those pastries. His precision left her speechless, and something in her shifted at that moment. She left quietly, wishing him well, and a heavy silence followed her out. What had begun as bitter competition slowly grew into mentorship and mutual respect. Years later, a chef once dismissed as capable of only one cuisine was celebrated for blending two.
①how food can turn hostility into meaningful pride
②an accident that reveals hospital safety was neglected
③how a rivalry, once repaired, grew into a cross-cultural friendship and shared achievement
④the reason French cuisine is considered superior to Indian cuisine
⑤a warning about the dangers of working in a restaurant kitchen

Across Vietnam a rice noodle dish is typically enjoyed for breakfast. The country is one of the largest rice producers in the world. That position comes from growing conditions that suit rice almost perfectly. Steamed rice is therefore a main staple food in Vietnamese cuisine. Rice is also made into noodles, served in a bowl of chicken, beef or seafood broth. A variety of spices and herbs gives the bowl a distinct Vietnamese flavor. Few dishes enjoy as much affection in Algeria as rechta does. The word descends from Persian rishta, which carries the sense of "thread" and is used broadly for wheat-flour noodles. True to that image, the noodles are cut thin and flat. To make them, Algerians combine wheat flour, salt, water, and ghee, the clarified butter their kitchens rely on. The finished bowl also carries chopped meat, onions, garlic, turnips, potatoes, zucchini, and spices particular to the country. It appears on the table at festive moments such as weddings and Eid al-Fitr, the feast ending Ramadan. What the bowl never holds is pork. Under Islamic dietary law pork is haram, forbidden, not halal, permissible, so the dish is built without it.

Rechta ranks among the dishes Algerians love most. Its name comes from the Persian word rishta, which means "thread" and usually refers to noodles made of wheat flour. The noodles used for it are thin and flat. Algerians make them by mixing wheat flour, salt, water, and ghee, a clarified butter, together. Chopped meat, onions, garlic, turnips, potatoes, zucchini, and uniquely Algerian spices fill out the dish. It is served on festive occasions, including weddings and Eid al-Fitr at the end of Ramadan. However, it is worth noting that rechta never contains pork. Islamic dietary law treats pork as haram, forbidden, rather than halal, permissible.

Across Peru, sopa criolla is a favorite choice at lunch or at dinner. Peruvians treat it as comfort food, and countless homes keep it as a staple. Its name translates as "creole soup," and creole points to local people usually descended from European conquerors. This suggests that Peruvian cuisine has been shaped not just by indigenous ethnic groups but also by foreign settlers. To make the soup, Peruvians normally use thin noodles, which are often called "angel hair." The noodles are boiled and served in a bowl of beef stock. Garlic, onions, tomato paste, and milk season the stock. A fried egg tops the bowl, which makes the dish look and taste delicious.

Rechta is one of the most popular Algerian dishes. The name originates from the Persian word rishta, which means "thread" and generally refers to noodles made of wheat flour. Rechta is made with thin and flat noodles. Algerians make the noodles by mixing wheat flour, salt, water, and ghee (clarified butter) together. The dish also contains ingredients such as chopped meat, onions, garlic, turnips, potatoes, zucchini, and uniquely Algerian spices. Algerians typically enjoy rechta on festive occasions, including weddings and Eid al-Fitr (the end of Ramadan). However, it is worth noting that rechta does not contain pork, as it is considered haram (forbidden), not halal (permissible), under Islamic dietary laws.

서술형 (본문 제시) · 5번
In Peru, people love to have sopa criolla for lunch or dinner. As a comfort food for Peruvians, it is a staple in many households. Sopa criolla means "creole soup," and the term creole refers to local people who are usually descendants of European conquerors. This suggests that Peruvian cuisine has been shaped not just by indigenous ethnic groups but also by foreign settlers. To make sopa criolla, Peruvians normally use thin noodles, which are often called "angel hair." Noodles are boiled and usually served in a bowl of beef stock seasoned with garlic, onions, tomato paste, milk, and other ingredients. The soup is often topped with a fried egg, which makes the dish look and taste delicious to Peruvians of all ages.

Madame Mallory pulled a package out of her basket—almond and apricot pastries. "Please, try one of my pastries," she said. I sat up, and she leaned over to adjust the pillows behind my back. "Tell me," she said, turning her back to me and again looking out the window, "what do you taste?" "Well, there's also a thin layer of nutmeg and pistachio paste, and the glaze is a coating made from egg yolks and honey." Madame Mallory could not find words. My answer had changed something in her. And when she did turn around, her eyes glistened like Spanish olives. Her expression told me that I possessed the culinary equivalent of perfect pitch. A few moments later, she was out the door again, and I immediately let out a sigh. Only after she was gone did I realize how incredibly tense I had been in her presence. His amazing sense of taste led him to harmonize the two cultures and create unique dishes. The story shows that what started as a feud between two cultures blossomed into a beautiful friendship and mutual understanding of cultures.
